explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Simon Peter answers, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." (Matthew 16:16) The crowd was tossing out names, and Peter just says it. No hedging, no "some say."

Elijah is on the list, but it's the crowd's list. The disciples tell Jesus that some say John the Baptist, others say Elijah, and still others Jeremiah or one of the prophets (Matthew 16:14). Then Jesus asks who the disciples say He is, and Simon Peter answers, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." (Matthew 16:16) Different question, different answer.

Close, because prophets fill up the crowd's answers, like "Jeremiah or one of the prophets." (Matthew 16:14) But that's what people say. When Jesus asks the disciples who they say He is, Simon Peter answers, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." (Matthew 16:16) That's not "one of the prophets," friend.

True. Right after Peter's answer, Jesus replies, "Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah!" (Matthew 16:17) He even uses the full name, Simon son of Jonah. When somebody uses my full name, I either sit up straight or check what I did. Here it comes with "Blessed."

Jesus does call him blessed. Peter says, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God," and Jesus replies, "Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah!" (Matthew 16:16-17) He doesn't brush it off or change the subject. He answers with a blessing, full name and all.

Jesus says it plainly: "this was not revealed to you by flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven." (Matthew 16:17) So it didn't come from a person. Jesus names His Father in heaven as the One who revealed it. That's a lot packed into one sentence, friend.

No angel in this verse, friend. Jesus says, "this was not revealed to you by flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven." (Matthew 16:17) He names His Father, and that's who gets the credit. I'll take what a verse says over a good guess any day.

Andrew is Peter's brother (Matthew 4:18), but Jesus says it wasn't flesh and blood. His words are, "this was not revealed to you by flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven." (Matthew 16:17) A brother, however close, is flesh and blood. Family can tell you plenty, but Jesus says this one came from His Father.

Jesus says the opposite. He says, "on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it." (Matthew 16:18) The little word is "not." Little word, big difference, friend.

That's it. Jesus says the gates of Hades "will not prevail against it," and "it" is the church He will build on this rock. (Matthew 16:18) He doesn't say the church barely squeaks by with a limp. He says the gates will not prevail.

explanations.answer: It will be loosed in heaven
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, "Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven." (Matthew 16:19) Bound goes with bound and loosed goes with loosed, like a cookie tin and its matching lid. He says it right after promising Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Both halves line up.

explanations.answer: It will be bound in heaven
explanations.explanation: Bound in heaven is the first half of the sentence, friend. Jesus says, "Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven." (Matthew 16:19) The second half switches the word, so loosed goes with loosed. It's easy to slide past when you read fast.

explanations.answer: It will be forgotten in heaven
explanations.explanation: Forgotten doesn't show up anywhere in this verse. Jesus says, "Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven." (Matthew 16:19) The second half matches the first: loosed on earth, loosed in heaven. Easy to remember, even for me, and I once spent ten minutes looking for the hat on my head.

It goes the other way, friend. Jesus admonished the disciples not to tell anyone that He was the Christ. (Matthew 16:20) Peter had just said it out loud, and then comes the hush. That's a secret big enough to fill a whole bakery.
That's right, it's the opposite. Then Jesus admonished the disciples not to tell anyone that He was the Christ. (Matthew 16:20) I'd have been bursting. Keeping quiet is not my best skill.

explanations.answer: He will be raised to life
explanations.explanation: Jesus says He must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things and be killed, and "on the third day be raised to life." (Matthew 16:21) I think this part is heavy, friend. But the last words He says are about being raised to life. He says them in the same breath as the hard part.
Galilee isn't in this verse. Jesus says He must be killed and "on the third day be raised to life." (Matthew 16:21) The verse tells us what happens on that third day, and it's being raised to life.

explanations.answer: He will appear in the temple
explanations.explanation: No temple appearance is in this verse. Jesus says He must go to Jerusalem and be killed, and "on the third day be raised to life." (Matthew 16:21) That's what the third day brings. It's the part to hold on to.

True. "Peter took Him aside and began to rebuke Him." (Matthew 16:22) He does it right after Jesus tells the disciples what's ahead. His words are, "Far be it from You, Lord!" and he calls Jesus Lord even while he's doing it.

He did. The verse says, "Peter took Him aside and began to rebuke Him." (Matthew 16:22) I bet it was one of those moments where the words came out faster than the thinking. Most of us have had one, friend.

Men. Jesus tells Peter, "you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men." (Matthew 16:23) Just a few verses earlier He called Peter blessed, and now this. I've had one oven give me a perfect batch and a rough one in the same afternoon, so I know how one source can give two very different results.
No kings in this verse, friend. Jesus says, "you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men." (Matthew 16:23) Kings sound fancy, but the verse is plainer than that. The word is men.

Priests do come up in this passage, just a verse earlier. Jesus says He will suffer at the hands of the elders, chief priests and scribes (Matthew 16:21). But that's a different list from this one. To Peter He says, "you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men." (Matthew 16:23)

His cross. Jesus says, "If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me." (Matthew 16:24) He's talking to His disciples. The invitation is for anyone who wants to come after Him.

A staff is a fine thing to carry on a walk, but this verse doesn't say staff. Jesus says anyone who wants to come after Him must "deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me." (Matthew 16:24) What gets taken up is a cross. That's the word He uses.

No sword in this verse, friend. Jesus says, "he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me." (Matthew 16:24) The cross is the thing He names. It's a quiet verse, and not a single sword gets drawn in it.

Jesus says, "whoever wants to save his life will lose it." (Matthew 16:25) Squeeze a ball of dough as hard as you can and it squishes out between your fingers. Different thing, same surprise: a tight grip doesn't always keep what you're holding. Jesus says it's the person who wants to save his life who loses it.

Not for the one who wants to save his life. Jesus says, "whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will find it." (Matthew 16:25) Forever isn't in the verse. The finding shows up in the second half, for the person who loses his life for His sake.

explanations.answer: He will win it back later
explanations.explanation: That sounds a lot like the second half of the verse. Jesus says, "whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will find it." (Matthew 16:25) The person who wants to save his life? He will lose it. The two halves go in opposite directions, baker.
Jesus says the opposite, friend. He says, "whoever loses his life for My sake will find it." (Matthew 16:25) Lose it for good isn't in there. The word He uses is find.

That's right, it's the other direction. Jesus says, "but whoever loses his life for My sake will find it." (Matthew 16:25) It comes right after the line about whoever wants to save his life losing it. Two halves, two directions, and this half ends with find.

True. Jesus asks, "What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul?" (Matthew 16:26) The whole world means every oven, every mixer, every cookie jar there is. The question sits right on what that man has gained and what he has forfeited.

Jesus does ask it. His words are, "What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul?" (Matthew 16:26) It comes as a question, right after He talks about losing and finding life (Matthew 16:25). The whole world and a soul are the two things in the question.

explanations.answer: Repay each one for what he has done
explanations.explanation: Jesus says the Son of Man will come in His Father's glory with His angels, and "then He will repay each one according to what he has done." (Matthew 16:27) Each one, friend. As for when, only the Father knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36), so I leave that part alone.

explanations.answer: Gather only His disciples to Him
explanations.explanation: Gathering isn't what this verse says. Jesus says, "then He will repay each one according to what he has done." (Matthew 16:27) The verse says each one, with no "only" in it. The thing He names is repaying.

No temple rebuilding in this verse. Jerusalem comes up in verse 21 as the place where Jesus must suffer (Matthew 16:21), but building isn't what He says here. Jesus says, "then He will repay each one according to what he has done." (Matthew 16:27) That's the thing He says He will do.

Jesus says some, not none. His words are, "Truly I tell you, some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom." (Matthew 16:28) One small word is the whole difference. Swap it out and you've got a different verse, friend.

False. Jesus says, "Truly I tell you, some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom." (Matthew 16:28) One little word, "some," and the whole answer flips. He doesn't say who or when there, so I won't guess either.
